text: QUBO is the single mathematical mold that almost every quantum optimization algorithm in this course is built to pour into. If you can write your problem in this form, QAOA, quantum annealers, and even many classical heuristics all have something concrete to run on.

QUBO stands for Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization, and each word matters. Quadratic means the cost function involves terms only up to degree two -- the cross terms x_i times x_j. Unconstrained means any of the 2 to the n binary strings is a legal candidate; real constraints still show up, just folded in as penalty terms. And binary means each variable is 0 or 1, not continuous -- which matters because for binary x_i, x_i squared equals x_i itself. That one small fact is exactly why a QUBO never needs higher-degree terms.

Here's a fully worked example. Take the matrix Q equal to negative 5, 2, 0, negative 3, giving f of x1, x2 equal to negative 5 x1 plus 2 x1 x2 minus 3 x2. Evaluating all four binary assignments directly: at 0,0 you get 0; at 0,1 you get negative 3; at 1,0 you get negative 5; and at 1,1 you get negative 5 plus 2 minus 3, equal to negative 6 -- the minimum. Selecting both variables wins, because the plus-2 interaction penalty isn't large enough to outweigh the combined rewards of negative 5 and negative 3.

Real problems have constraints, like 'pick exactly 2 of 5 assets.' QUBO has no native syntax for that, so you add a penalty term: P times the quantity sum of x_i minus B, squared. That expression is zero exactly when the constraint holds, and strictly positive the moment it's violated. Choose P large enough, and the minimizer is steered toward constraint-satisfying solutions without ever writing an explicit 'subject to' clause.

Next lesson makes a connection every quantum optimization algorithm in this course depends on: converting this QUBO into the Ising model -- the same optimization landscape, described in the language quantum hardware actually speaks.
